name: Agent: Web Development
summary: Turns a Figma design into a real page that matches it — fast, accessible, and a proper page in every language it ships in.
objectives: Turn a Figma design into a real page that matches it — and prove the match, instead of eyeballing it.
A page that misses the quality bar does not ship. The gate decides, not an opinion.
Every language is its own real page that Google can find — not text swapped in by a script.

outcomes.text: It built a landing page from one design frame and put it live in two languages. Each language is a real page that points at the other, so a search engine finds both.
The page scores 97, 97, 100 and 100 on Google's own quality test — speed, accessibility, best practice, SEO. The bar to ship is 90 on all four.
Nobody types SEO into the code. It is generated from the project's own data, and a console lets someone who does not code review and fix it before launch.
Each language gets its own preview card for when someone shares the link — in that language. The picture has words on it, so the words get translated too.

Matching the design is measured three ways instead of one. A single "percent different" score never reaches zero once there are photographs on the page — and a bar nobody can clear is a bar everybody ignores.

An independent check went looking for holes in the agent and found five. All five are closed — including a test that had been written but never actually run, so the gate that stops a below-standard page from shipping was itself unwatched. It runs on every change now.

A second check re-examined the agent after those fixes. It re-ran the original tests to prove all five earlier findings are truly closed, and found fourteen more — including one that matters: the check meant to refuse an incomplete brief accepts an empty one.

All fourteen are now closed. The brief check refuses an empty brief. Two quality checks that had been named in the checklist but never actually written now exist, and one of them immediately caught a real accessibility miss on the live page that nobody had ever measured.

The bigger change: the checklist can no longer lie. Seven items claimed an automatic check that did not exist — and since the human reviewer walks only the manual ones, nobody checked them. Every automatic item must now name its check, or the tests refuse the change.

A fourth check graded the third instead of taking its word for it, re-running the original test behind each of its fourteen fixes. Thirteen hold. The fourteenth was fixed here but not inside the agent folder, so anyone copying the agent elsewhere still has it.

It used two reviewers who could not see each other's work: one reads the agent's rules, one was handed the code with every rule document removed, so it had to judge whether the code is right rather than whether it matches. Fourteen finds, and they agreed on two.

The costliest find is one no rule could point at: the check that scores page quality never noticed the tool it runs had failed, and read the leftover results of the previous run. It reported four perfect scores for a page it never loaded.

All fourteen of those were fixed, and the fix was written as a rule instead of as fourteen patches: every check must now say out loud how much it actually looked at, and its own tests hold it to the number.
A fifth check graded those fixes by re-running the original test behind each one, rather than reading the write-up of the person who made them. All fourteen hold.

That same check found twenty new problems, and this is the useful part: the new rule was followed to the letter and still missed. One check reports examining 23 things out of 104 and calls it a pass, because it only asks whether the number is zero — not whether it is enough.

The two reviewers overlapped on one problem out of twenty, and each found a serious one the other never saw — a quality check that reads a fraction of the page and calls it clean, and a design-match check that the number printed in its own instructions switches off entirely.

Fixing what a check finds has created roughly as many new problems as it closed, four rounds running. That is now a measured trend rather than an impression, and breaking it is worth more than any single item on the list.

All twenty are closed. The check that read 23 things out of 104 now reads 104 out of 111 — because it scrolls the page first, which it never did — and it hands a person 35 items it cannot judge instead of 6.

The rule that missed was made specific instead of repeated: every check now reports what it examined as a fraction of what was there, and a small fraction fails. Printing a number was not enough — the number needed something to be a fraction of.

The page's share-preview cards could not be rebuilt at all — the template pointed at a picture a redesign had deleted, and every check passed because they all inspect the finished card. The gate now rebuilds them, so a broken generator cannot hide behind a file that already exists.

Three and a half megabytes of images that no page ever showed were shipping with the project — 60% of its picture weight, on a page whose single biggest speed lever is exactly that. They are gone, and a new check lists any file nothing points at.

These fixes were deliberately not graded by the people who made them. One of the ten questions the work opened is real: now that the accessibility check reads the whole page, it finds seven contrast misses — all the brand orange a person already chose to keep, with nowhere to record that choice.

A sixth check graded those twenty fixes by undoing each one in a scratch copy, to see whether the test everyone relied on actually turns red. All twenty hold. Three of the tests behind them do not: one covers half its claim, one catches only that fix's exact wording, and one does not exist.

The rule written to stop a check passing after seeing only a fraction of the page compares two different things. On the agent's own pages it reports examining more items than exist — 107 out of 101 — so the floor can never trigger. It looked right on the one page it was built against.

Copying the agent for a new client and deleting the previous client's project — the first thing anyone would do — breaks the agent's own self-test. A single line reaches into that example project, and because the tests stop at the first failure, eight of the twelve then never run at all.
The check was pointed at the agent's own tools for the first time. The console people use to review a page's SEO before launch fails the accessibility bar the agent enforces on everything it builds.

The two independent reviewers agreed on two findings out of forty-three, and on none of the ten about the example project. A single reviewer finds about a quarter of what is there, and which quarter depends on whether they may read the rules. Both serious findings came from the one who could.

milestones.title: Write the rules: layout, screen sizes, dark mode, SEO, languages and the quality gate
Make an approved brief a hard gate — no build starts without one
Turn the quality checks into code that can stop a delivery
Build the first landing page from a real design
Ship it in two languages, each a real page
Generate the SEO instead of hand-writing it, with a console for people who do not code
Feed what the first project taught back into the rules
Set the agent up in the shared workspace, so anyone can start a project with it
Have the agent independently checked, and turn what it found into fixes
Fix what the second check opened, starting with the brief check that accepts an empty brief
Fix what the third and fourth checks found, starting with the quality score that can be reported for a page that was never loaded
Have a sixth check grade those twenty fixes, and say whether the pattern actually broke
Break the pattern where each round of fixes seeds the next round of problems — six rounds in, it has not broken yet
Fix what the sixth check found, starting with the two problems that travel to every copy of the agent
Decide how a deliberate exception — a brand colour kept below the accessibility bar — gets recorded where the check can see it
